beginner: Garlic likes loose, rich soil that drains well but still holds some moisture, with plenty of compost worked in. Loosen the bed deeply before planting so the roots and bulbs have room. The thing it cannot stand is soggy, waterlogged ground, which rots the cloves over winter, so avoid heavy clay and any low spot where water sits.
seasoned: Garlic grows in most soils but does best in a loose, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter. Because the crop sits in the ground from fall through the next summer, drainage over winter is the make-or-break factor: cloves in cold, saturated soil rot before spring. Work in generous compost and loosen the bed deeply before planting, and on heavy ground plant in raised beds or rows so the bulb zone never stays waterlogged.

beginner: Garlic grows best in soil close to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. It is not very fussy, but very acidic ground holds it back, so if a soil test reads below about 6.0, mix in some garden lime before you plant in fall.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; garlic tolerates a slightly wider band, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but yields fall off on strongly acidic soils. Test the bed the season before and lime an acid plot up toward neutral, since fall is your one planting window and there is no second chance to adjust mid-season.

beginner: Garlic is a hungry plant that makes its bulb from the leaves it grows in spring, so feed it then. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil when you plant in fall, then give it a nitrogen feeding once the green shoots are growing well in early spring, and again a few weeks later. Stop feeding before the bulbs start sizing up, which falls around April in warm regions and into May where winters are cold. Feeding late makes leafy plants with thick necks and small bulbs that do not keep well.
seasoned: Garlic has a moderate to high nitrogen demand and builds its bulb on the leaves it grows in spring, so feeding is front-loaded onto the spring vegetative push. Mix a complete fertilizer or compost into the bed at fall planting, then side-dress nitrogen as the shoots resume growth in early spring and again two to three weeks later. The exact cutoff tracks your season rather than a fixed calendar date. In cold-winter regions with a later crop, the last feedings run later: Utah State suggests about half a pound of 21-0-0 per 100 square feet in mid-April with a quarter pound in late May, and the University of Minnesota feeds through spring growth before bulbing. In the warm Southeast, where the crop runs weeks earlier, UGA advises no nitrogen after the first week of April. The unifying rule is to stop nitrogen several weeks before bulbing begins, since late feeding delays bulbing, thickens necks, and worsens storage.

beginner: Feed your garlic some nitrogen now, while it is growing leaves in spring.
seasoned: Side-dress your garlic with nitrogen now to drive spring leaf growth before bulbing.

beginner: Use a feed higher in the first number (nitrogen) such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer in spring, then stop by early May.
seasoned: Higher first-number (N) feeds in spring, e.g. ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) or blood meal; taper off and stop by early May so bulbing is not delayed.

beginner: About half a pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate per 100 square feet in early spring, then a lighter feeding a few weeks later, following the package directions.
seasoned: About half a pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet as shoots resume in spring, with a lighter follow-up two to three weeks later; finish before early May.

beginner: Garlic is famous as a good-neighbor plant, mostly because its strong smell is thought to keep aphids and some other pests away, so it is often tucked among roses, fruit trees, tomatoes, and cabbage-family plants. The one thing to keep it away from is beans and peas, since garlic and its onion relatives are believed to slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
seasoned: Garlic's companion reputation rests almost entirely on its sulfur scent, traditionally credited with deterring aphids, spider mites, and some borers, which is why it is interplanted among roses, fruit trees, tomatoes, and brassicas. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep garlic away from them. Most of these pairings are traditional rather than trial-proven, and garlic's long fall-to-summer occupancy means it shares the bed with whatever overwinters or goes in around it; treat the pairings as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

beginner: Garlic's strong smell is thought to help keep aphids and spider mites off tomatoes, and the two fit together in the bed because garlic is finishing up in early summer as tomatoes take off.
seasoned: Tomatoes are a traditional garlic companion on the allium pest-repel reputation, the scent said to discourage aphids and spider mites, plus a tidy timing fit: fall-planted garlic is sizing and harvested in early summer just as tomatoes need the room. The pest claim is folk wisdom rather than a tested effect, but the pairing is low-risk and space-efficient.

beginner: Garlic is a classic underplanting for roses and fruit trees, where its smell is believed to help fend off aphids and borers. It takes little room and is harvested before midsummer.
seasoned: Underplanting roses and fruit trees with garlic is a long-standing tradition, the pungent foliage credited with deterring aphids and some borers. It is a space-and-scent pairing rather than a demonstrated effect; garlic's small footprint and early-summer harvest make it an easy, low-competition neighbor for perennials.

beginner: Cabbage-family plants share garlic's cool-season liking, and the strong garlic smell is thought to bother some of their pests like aphids and cabbage worms.
seasoned: Brassicas are interplanted with garlic on the same allium-scent logic used for onions: the sulfur smell is traditionally credited with masking the cabbage family from aphids and caterpillars. Garlic is shallow and undemanding, so it tucks between cole crops without competing, though the pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-proven for garlic.

beginner: Garlic grows alongside carrots and beets without crowding them, and its smell is said to help confuse pests like the carrot rust fly. They use different space above and below ground.
seasoned: Carrots and beets pair with garlic on complementary form and the allium scent-masking tradition, the same logic behind the well-known carrot-and-onion pairing against carrot rust fly. Garlic sends a narrow bulb down with little leafy spread, so it shares space efficiently. The scent-masking effect is best evidenced for onions; for garlic treat it as a reasonable, low-risk extension.

beginner: Keep garlic away from beans and peas. Garlic and its onion relatives are long believed to slow the growth of these legumes, so plant them in separate parts of the garden.
seasoned: Beans and peas are the standard allium caution: garlic, like onion, is traditionally held to inhibit legume growth, so the two are kept apart. The mechanism is not firmly established, but the recommendation is consistent across companion guidance, so separate garlic from beans and peas as a low-cost precaution.

beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often hiding in the tight folds where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaves and down in the leaf folds; heavy feeding in warm, dry spells reduces bulb size.

beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry weather and shelter in the leaf axils where sprays miss them; they move readily between alliums.

beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant garlic where onions or garlic grew last year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.
seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, use reflective mulch, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.

beginner: Plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet weather.
seasoned: Wilting, yellowing plants and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet conditions and where allium debris carries the pest over.

beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of the plants. They survive in leftover onion and garlic debris.
seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue and cull bulbs.

beginner: Do not plant garlic in the same place each year, and clean up old onion and garlic scraps where the fly breeds.
seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull bulbs and crop residue, and avoid planting into fresh manure; cultural sanitation is the main home-garden tool.

beginner: Plants are stunted and yellow and die back early. The bulbs turn brown, shrivel, feel light, and their papery skins crack and peel away from the base. The damage keeps getting worse in storage.
seasoned: Stunting, distortion, yellowing, and premature dieback of leaves, with swollen, distorted stems and bulbs; infected bulbs turn brown, shrivel, go lightweight, and the wrapper layers crack and detach from the basal plate, with damage progressing in storage.

beginner: A microscopic worm that lives and feeds inside the leaves, stems, and bulbs. It usually arrives on infected cloves you plant and can survive dried in the soil for years.
seasoned: The stem and bulb nematode (Ditylenchus dipsaci), the garlic bloat nematode, a microscopic worm that feeds inside the leaves, stems, and bulbs. It rides in on infected planting cloves and survives dried in soil and debris for at least four years, favored by cool, moist conditions.

beginner: Start with clean, healthy cloves from a trusted source, since this is how the worm usually arrives. Do not grow garlic or onions in that spot for four years, and pull and throw away any infected plants. Crops like carrots, potatoes, and corn are safe to grow there in between.
seasoned: Plant only clean, tested, nematode-free seed stock, the single most important practice; rotate garlic out for four years with poor-host crops (carrots, potatoes, spinach, corn, wheat); remove and destroy infected plants and debris. Hot-water seed dips are no longer recommended because they only reduce, not eliminate, the nematode.

beginner: The plant yellows and wilts from the bottom and pulls out of the ground easily. You find white fuzzy mold and tiny black specks on the rotting roots and bulb.
seasoned: Leaves decay at the base, yellow, wilt, and topple, and the plant pulls up easily; a fluffy white mold and tiny black sclerotia about the size of a poppy seed form on the rotting roots and bulb. It is the most serious soilborne disease of garlic.

beginner: A soil fungus that makes tiny long-lived resting bodies that can sit in the ground for years and attack in cool weather. It spreads on dirty tools, soil, and infected cloves.
seasoned: The fungus Sclerotium cepivorum, which produces hardy sclerotia that survive in soil for many years and germinate in the cool soils garlic grows in (activity is restricted above about 75°F). It spreads on contaminated soil, tools, and infected cloves.

beginner: There is no fix once it is in the soil, so prevention is key. Plant only clean cloves in clean ground, do not move soil from an infected bed, pull and destroy sick plants, and keep alliums out of that spot for years.
seasoned: There is no cure once soil is infested. Plant only disease-free cloves in clean soil, never move contaminated soil into new ground, remove and destroy infected plants, and use long allium-free rotations; the fungus persists for years, so prevention is everything.

beginner: Leaves yellow and die back and the plant is stunted. The bottom of the bulb turns brown and rots, and the decay works its way up into the bulb.
seasoned: Yellowing and dieback of leaves, stunting, and a brown dry rot that starts at the basal plate (the root end) and spreads up into the bulb, which becomes pitted; roots die back and bulbs rot in the field and in storage.

beginner: A soil fungus that lives in the ground for years and does the most damage in warm soil. Injuries and infected cloves let it in.
seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium oxysporum (including f. sp. cepae) and related species that persist in soil for years and progress fastest in warm soils (about 77 to 82°F); wounds, maggot feeding, and infected cloves open the door.

beginner: Plant healthy cloves, do not grow garlic in the same spot for several years, handle the bulbs gently so they are not injured, and store them cool and dry.
seasoned: Plant clean, tested cloves, rotate out of alliums for several years, avoid wounding bulbs, store cured bulbs cool (below about 39°F) and dry, and choose less-susceptible stock where available.

beginner: Garlic goes soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, often with a gray mold. It mostly hits bulbs that were not dried well or were picked too green.
seasoned: A soft, water-soaked rot starting at the neck after harvest, with a gray mold on or between the scales and later small black sclerotia; poorly cured, thick-necked, or immature bulbs are most affected.

beginner: A mold that gets into the necks of garlic that was harvested too green or dried poorly. Too much late fertilizer and wet weather near harvest make it worse.
seasoned: Botrytis species that overwinter on debris and infected bulbs and as sclerotia in soil; excess late nitrogen, rain or irrigation late in the season, and inadequate curing or storage all worsen it.

beginner: Stop feeding by early May, stop watering before harvest, dry (cure) the garlic well until the necks are tight, and store it cool, dry, and airy.
seasoned: Stop nitrogen by early May, cut water before harvest, cure thoroughly until necks are tight and dry, handle gently, and store cool and dry with good airflow.

beginner: Little orange or rusty spots and bumps on the leaves. Usually minor, but a bad case yellows the leaves early and makes smaller bulbs. It likes cool, damp, crowded plantings.
seasoned: Small orange to rust-colored pustules scattered on the leaves, which in heavy cases yellow and die back early and reduce bulb size; usually a minor problem but worse in cool, humid, crowded plantings, notably in coastal and mild-winter areas.

beginner: A rust fungus that spreads in cool, damp weather through wet leaves and splashing water.
seasoned: A Puccinia rust fungus favored by cool temperatures, leaf wetness, and high humidity; spores spread on wind and splashing water and overwinter on volunteer alliums.

beginner: Give plants room for air to move, water at the base, do not over-fertilize, and pull out badly spotted leaves and any volunteer onions or garlic nearby. It is usually minor.
seasoned: Space for airflow, avoid overhead watering and excess nitrogen, remove volunteer alliums and badly infected leaves, and rotate; rust is usually minor enough that cultural steps suffice in the home garden.

beginner: Water garlic regularly in spring so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly an inch a week. Then stop watering a couple of weeks before harvest so the bulbs can dry down and the skins set.
seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist through spring leaf growth and bulbing, about an inch of water per week including rain. Then taper and stop watering about two weeks before harvest so the bulbs firm up and the wrappers cure clean.

beginner: About one inch of water a week while the plants are growing in spring, and a bit more in warm, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
seasoned: Roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation through the spring growing season; more in warm, dry, or sandy conditions, delivered steadily rather than in swings.

beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent disease.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; wet leaves and standing water feed the leaf and bulb rots garlic is prone to.

beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Garlic sitting in wet soil rots.
seasoned: Yellowing, soft lower leaves and a sour smell signal waterlogging; saturated soil over winter and at bulbing drives white rot, basal rot, and neck rot.

beginner: Wilting, blue-tinged, or brown-tipped leaves in spring mean the garlic is too dry. Garlic that dries out while sizing makes smaller bulbs.
seasoned: Bluish, tip-burned, or prematurely dying leaves and stalled growth mean the bulbs are short of water during the spring sizing window, which caps final bulb size.

beginner: After planting the cloves in fall, water once to settle the soil. Over winter garlic mostly takes care of itself, so do not keep the bed soggy in cold weather.
seasoned: Water the cloves in at fall planting to settle the soil and start root growth, then let fall rain and winter carry them; dormant garlic under mulch needs little supplemental water and should not sit wet in cold soil.

beginner: When green shoots come up in spring, start watering again to keep the soil evenly damp. Do not let it get soggy while the soil is still cold.
seasoned: As shoots push up in late winter and spring, resume even moisture; the bed should not dry out once active growth restarts, but avoid waterlogging still-cold soil.

beginner: As the leaves grow fast in spring, keep the soil evenly damp, about 1 inch of water a week. Those leaves turn into the bulb wrappers, so do not let the bed dry out.
seasoned: Spring leaf growth is water-sensitive: keep the bed evenly moist at about an inch a week, since every leaf now becomes a bulb wrapper later. Never let it dry out through this stretch.

beginner: Keep watering evenly, about 1 inch a week, while the bulbs get bigger. This is when the size is set. Near the end, start easing off as harvest gets close.
seasoned: Keep steady moisture as bulbs size up, about an inch a week; this is the yield-setting window. Toward the end of bulbing, begin tapering as harvest approaches.

beginner: Stop watering about two weeks before you dig the garlic. A dry finish makes firm bulbs with clean, tight skins that store well, while watering right up to harvest makes soft bulbs that do not keep.
seasoned: Cut water off about two weeks before harvest. Letting the bed dry firms the bulbs and cures the wrappers tight; watering into harvest gives soft bulbs and stained, split wrappers that store poorly.

beginner: Do not water. After digging, dry the bulbs in an airy, shady spot for a few weeks. Any moisture now can cause rot in storage.
seasoned: No watering. Cure the bulbs out of the ground in a dry, airy, shaded spot for a few weeks; moisture now invites rot in storage.

beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to catch the diseases that make garlic rot in storage.
seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for garlic because lingering leaf wetness and saturated soil feed the storage rots that spoil bulbs after harvest.

beginner: The most important time to water is during spring growth and while the bulbs are sizing up. Then stop about two weeks before harvest so the bulbs dry down properly.
seasoned: Spring leaf growth and bulb sizing are the water-sensitive weeks; never let the bed dry out then. Equally important is cutting water off about two weeks before harvest so the wrappers cure tight.

beginner: Not needed. You plant garlic straight in the garden from cloves in fall, so there are no seedlings to harden off. Just split a bulb into individual cloves right before planting and put the biggest ones in pointy side up.
seasoned: Not applicable. Garlic is planted directly in the ground from cloves in fall, not raised as transplants, so there is no indoor start or hardening-off step. Break a bulb into cloves just before planting and set the largest ones, papery wrappers intact, pointed end up.

beginner: Garlic does not grow from seed, you plant the cloves. Just before planting in fall, break a bulb into separate cloves and leave the papery skin on each one. Plant the biggest cloves pointy side up, about 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. Big cloves grow big bulbs, so plant the largest and cook with the little ones. Start with healthy cloves from a trusted source so you do not bring in disease.
seasoned: Garlic is grown from cloves, not seed. Break apart firm, healthy bulbs into individual cloves just before planting, keep the papery skins on, and plant the largest cloves pointed end up about 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fall. Bigger cloves make bigger bulbs, so save the largest for planting and eat the small inner ones. Use clean, disease-free seed stock from a reputable source, since white rot and bloat nematode ride in on infected cloves.

beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer. Garlic should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil rots the cloves, especially over winter.
seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; garlic must never sit in standing water, which saturates the bulb zone over winter and rots the cloves.

beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
seasoned: A free-draining potting mix blended with compost.

beginner: Mix in compost, and a little slow-release fertilizer at planting helps.
seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a slow-release balanced feed at planting; keep the mix free-draining for the long overwinter.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check often in spring growth, but do not keep the mix soggy over winter or the cloves rot.
seasoned: Expect to water more often than in-ground during spring growth; the shallow pot volume dries quickly and a drought check at sizing shrinks bulbs. Keep the mix on the dry side over winter to avoid clove rot.

beginner: Because watering washes food out of pots, feed container garlic a little more often through spring, then stop by early May.
seasoned: Frequent spring watering leaches nutrients, so feed container garlic lightly but regularly through leaf growth, then stop by early May as in the ground.

beginner: Garlic in a pot is meant to overwinter, since you plant it in fall and harvest the next summer. In cold areas the roots in a pot freeze harder than in the ground, so sink the pot, move it against the house or into an unheated shed or cold frame, or mulch it well, and let it freeze and rest rather than trying to keep it growing.
seasoned: Overwintering is the whole point of a garlic container: fall-planted, it sits dormant through winter and finishes the next summer. The limited root volume of a pot freezes colder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or heap mulch around it; the goal is to carry the cloves safely through the cold, not to force winter growth.

beginner: Garlic grows fine in a deep pot because its roots are not huge. Use a container at least 8 inches deep with drainage holes, plant cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and plan to leave it out all winter. Keep it watered in spring and stop a couple of weeks before harvest.
seasoned: Garlic is workable in containers given depth and drainage. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep, 3 gallons or more, set cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and treat it as a year-long resident: it overwinters in the pot and matures the next summer. Containers dry fast in spring, so water steadily through bulbing, then cut water two weeks before harvest. The main risk is winter waterlogging in a pot that drains poorly.

beginner: Skip a self-watering pot for garlic. It keeps the soil too wet for a crop that sits all winter and needs to dry out before harvest, which can rot the bulbs. A regular pot with drainage holes that you water yourself is better.
seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor match for garlic: the constantly moist reservoir keeps the bulb zone too wet over the long overwinter and during the curing-down before harvest, both of which invite clove and bulb rot. A free-draining pot you water on demand is safer.

beginner: Do not plant garlic where you grew garlic, onions, or leeks recently. The diseases and the nematode that hit garlic live in the soil for years and build up, so wait about 4 years before alliums return to the same spot.
seasoned: Do not follow garlic or other alliums (onion, leek, shallot, chives) in the same ground. Garlic's worst soilborne problems, white rot and bloat nematode, persist for years and build up under continuous alliums; extension guidance is to rotate garlic out for about 4 years.

beginner: Keep moving garlic around the garden. Wait about 4 years before planting garlic, onions, or leeks in the same spot, because soil diseases and the nematode build up there. Following garlic with crops like carrots, potatoes, or corn, which the nematode does not feed on, helps clean the ground.
seasoned: Rotate so garlic and its allium relatives do not return to the same bed for about 4 years. White rot sclerotia survive in soil for years and bloat nematode persists in debris, so a long rotation away from the whole family is the core defense. Carrots, potatoes, spinach, corn, and grains are good rotation crops because they are poor hosts for the bloat nematode.

beginner: Once the garlic is cured (dried), keep the bulbs somewhere cool, dry, and airy, out of the light. A cool pantry works for a while; a steady cool spot keeps them longest. Damp or warm places make garlic sprout and soften.
seasoned: After curing, store cured bulbs in a cool, dry, airy place. The classic storage range is cool and dry, around 32 to 40°F for long holding, though many cooks simply keep braids or bulbs at a cool room temperature out of light. Warm, humid spots and the 40 to 60°F range encourage sprouting.

beginner: Do not store whole garlic bulbs in the fridge. The cold, damp air actually makes them sprout. Keep cured bulbs in a cool, dry cupboard instead. You can refrigerate a few peeled cloves for a day or two if it is handy.
seasoned: Whole cured bulbs store poorly in the refrigerator: the 40 to 50°F, humid environment is exactly what triggers sprouting, so keep them cool and dry instead. Peeled cloves can be refrigerated briefly for convenience.

beginner: You can peel and chop garlic and freeze it for cooking. It goes soft after thawing, so use frozen garlic in cooked food, not raw.
seasoned: Garlic freezes well peeled and chopped, or as a puree, for cooking; texture softens, so use frozen garlic in cooked dishes rather than raw.

beginner: How long garlic keeps depends on the type and how well you dried it. Softneck garlics (the braiding kinds) keep longest, often six to nine months. Hardneck garlics taste stronger but keep a shorter time, often four to six months, so eat those first. Drying the bulbs well is the most important thing for good storage.
seasoned: Storage life tracks type and curing. Well-cured softneck types (artichoke, silverskin) keep the longest, commonly six to nine months or more, which is why they are the braiding and grocery-store garlics. Hardneck types are richer-flavored but shorter-keeping, often about four to six months. Good curing, dry necks and papery wrappers, is the single biggest lever on how long any garlic keeps.

beginner: Pick the type that matches your winters first. In cold-winter areas, grow hardneck garlic (like Music, Spanish Roja, or Chesnok Red), which needs real cold, makes big cloves, and gives you edible scapes, but does not store as long. In mild-winter and southern areas, grow softneck garlic (like Inchelium Red or California Early), which handles warm winters, makes lots of cloves, braids nicely, and keeps the longest. If you are not sure, Inchelium Red is forgiving in many climates. Elephant garlic is not really garlic, it is a mild leek relative.
seasoned: Choose by winter cold first, then by use. Hardneck garlics (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe groups, such as Music, German White, Spanish Roja, Chesnok Red) need a genuine cold winter to vernalize and bulb, produce edible scapes, have fewer larger cloves, and store a shorter time, so they shine in the North. Softneck garlics (Artichoke and Silverskin groups, such as Inchelium Red, California Early and Late, Creole and Silverskin types) tolerate mild winters, yield more smaller cloves, braid well, and store the longest, so they are the choice for the South and warm regions. Where winters are mild, lean softneck; where winters are cold, hardnecks reward you with flavor. Elephant garlic is a leek relative, not true garlic.

beginner: After you plant the cloves in fall, they grow roots underground and may send up a small green shoot before winter. This is normal. The garlic is settling in and starting to feel the cold it needs, not making big leaves yet.
seasoned: In fall you set cloves pointed end up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. Over the next few weeks roots grow and a small shoot may push up before cold sets in; the cloves are anchoring and beginning to vernalize, not yet making top growth.

beginner: Plant the cloves at the right time for your area and water them in. In cold regions, once the ground begins to freeze, cover the bed with a few inches of straw or chopped leaves to protect the cloves over winter.
seasoned: Plant on time for your zone, water in, and once the ground starts to freeze in cold regions cover the bed with 3 to 4 inches of straw or shredded-leaf mulch to buffer the soil through winter and prevent freeze-thaw heaving.

beginner: Write down when you planted, which kind of garlic, and how big the cloves were. It helps you do better next year.
seasoned: Record your planting date, variety, and clove size; over seasons this is the best predictor of bulb size and timing for your site.

beginner: In cold areas the garlic mostly rests under its mulch all winter. In mild areas it keeps growing slowly. When spring arrives, green shoots come up and the plant starts making leaves.
seasoned: Through winter the plant is largely dormant under mulch in cold regions, or grows slowly in mild ones. As soil warms in late winter to early spring, green shoots emerge or resume and the plant begins building leaves, the leaves that will become bulb wrappers.

beginner: In spring, loosen the winter mulch if it is soggy, start feeding nitrogen as the shoots grow, and keep weeds pulled, because weeds easily crowd out young garlic.
seasoned: In spring, pull mulch back if it is matting wet over the crowns, begin nitrogen feeding as shoots resume, and keep the bed weed-free; garlic competes poorly with weeds and early weed control protects yield.

beginner: Write down when the green shoots came up in spring and when you first fed the plants.
seasoned: Note when shoots emerged or resumed and your first spring feeding; emergence timing tracks how your winter ran.

beginner: The garlic grows lots of upright leaves in spring. This stage matters most for bulb size, because the leaves now turn into the layers of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves it grows, the bigger the bulb can be.

beginner: Write down how long you dried the garlic and how well it kept, so you know how long to cure next time.

beginner: Garlic is one of the easiest crops to grow, but it works on an unusual schedule. You plant the cloves in fall, they rest through winter (under a mulch blanket where it is cold), and they finish growing the next summer, so a single planting takes most of a year. Garlic needs that winter cold to form a proper bulb, which is why you plant in fall rather than spring. Grow hardneck garlic where winters are cold and softneck garlic where they are mild.
seasoned: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves planted in fall. It roots before winter, overwinters in the ground (mulched in cold regions), then resumes growth in spring and matures the following summer, an eight to nine month crop that spans the year. Winter cold is essential: cloves must be vernalized to divide and bulb properly, which is why fall planting beats spring. Hardneck types suit cold winters, produce edible scapes, and store a few months; softneck types suit mild climates, braid well, and store the longest.

beginner: Garlic is ready in early summer (or late spring in warm areas) when the lower leaves have turned brown but the top leaves are still green, about a third to half of them browned. Do not wait for all the leaves to die. Dig one bulb to check: if the cloves fill out the skins, it is time to harvest.
seasoned: Garlic is ready in early to mid summer (late spring in warm regions) when the lower leaves have browned and died back while several upper leaves stay green, about a third to half the foliage turned. Each green leaf is an intact wrapper, so do not wait for all the leaves to brown. Confirm by lifting a test bulb: ready bulbs have cloves that fill the skins.
